The number of Indian students studying in the United States declined by 6.5% to 339,435 in the 2025–26 academic year, marking the first annual decline since 2020–21, even as India retained its position as the largest source of international students in the country for the third consecutive year, according to a report by the Institute of International Education (IIE), a New York-based NGO.
It was released to the public on Monday. HT was given early access to a copy of the report.

According to the report, titled Open Doors Report on International Educational Exchange, the latest decline was driven largely by a 34% drop in Indian students pursuing graduate programmes, whose numbers fell from 177,892 in 2024–25 to 116,609. Undergraduate enrolments also dipped marginally to 39,711 from 40,135. However, the number of Indian students participating in OPT, which allows international graduates to gain work experience in the US after completing their degrees, rose 27% to 182,201.
Indian student enrolments in the US had last declined in 2020–21, falling to 167,582 from 193,124 in the previous year. They subsequently rose for four consecutive years, reaching a peak of 363,019 in 2024–25, before reversing the trend this year. The report also showed that China , the second-largest source of international students in the US, also recorded a decline, with its numbers falling 4% to 254,458 from 265,919 in 2024–25. Overall, US colleges and universities hosted 1,146,163 international students in 2025–26, down around 3% from 1,177,766 in the previous academic year.
Across all academic levels, 57% of international students were enrolled in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) fields. Mathematics and computer science, with 286,168 students, and engineering, with 214,193, were the most popular fields.
Meanwhile, OPT participation among international students rose 14% to 335,785. The number of new international students — those enrolling at a US institution for the first time — fell 18% to 228,123.
The report’s fall 2026 snapshot, based on responses from more than 800 US higher education institutions, points to a further slowdown. Overall international student numbers declined 9%, with new enrolments falling 15%. Graduate enrolments dropped 15%, undergraduate numbers 3% and OPT participation 6%. The decline comes amid tightening US immigration measures and visa-related uncertainties.

HT reported on October 23 that arrivals of Indian students in the US on F and M category visas had plunged 39% year-on-year to 25,321 in August 2026.
Experts and study-abroad consultants cited stricter visa screening, delays in appointments and processing, higher rejection rates and uncertainty over post-study employment opportunities, including OPT, as factors affecting student mobility.
Sanjay Maurya is a Principal Correspondent with Hindustan Times, where he covers education, with a focus on school and higher education, competitive examinations, education policy and governance. Working as part of the National Bureau, he is based in New Delhi and reports on the Ministry of Education and covers various statutory bodies like UGC, AICTE and NCTE and autonomous bodies like CBSE and NCERT. His reporting also tracks the implementation of key government reforms and policies from school education to higher education including in IITs, NITs, IIMs, central and state universities, and their impact on students and educational institutions. His reporting on the irregularities and rushed implementation of CBSE's On-Screen Marking (OSM) system for evaluation of Class 12 board exams 2026, triggered administrative action, leading to the transfer of the board's two senior-most officials and the constitution of a committee to probe alleged irregularities in procurement process of the system. He joined Hindustan Times in December 2024. Prior to that, he had a three-year stint at Careers360, where he reported on school and higher education, entrance examinations, admissions, rankings and various education policies involving universities and professional education bodies. Over the years, Maurya has reported extensively on major developments in India's education sector, including the implementation of the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, reforms in the National Testing Agency (NTA) following the NEET-UG 2024 controversy, changes in school education, higher education regulation, and the evolution of entrance examinations such as NEET, JEE and CUET. He regularly produces data-driven and explanatory stories based on government documents, parliamentary proceedings, court records and official data.
